title: Is your baby ready for solid food?
summary: The three signs to look for, usually at around 6 months.

paragraphs: The NHS recommends starting solid food at around 6 months, alongside breast milk or first infant formula. Look for three signs together:
bullets: They can stay in a sitting position, holding their head steady.
They can coordinate their eyes, hands and mouth: look at food, pick it up and put it in their mouth.
They can swallow food rather than spit it back out.

sections.heading: Not signs of readiness
paragraphs: Chewing fists, wanting extra milk feeds and waking more at night are normal at this age and don't mean a baby needs solid food.

sections.heading: Born early
paragraphs: Ask your health visitor or GP when to start weaning a baby who was born early.

checklist.text: Sits up holding their head steady
Looks at food, picks it up and puts it in their mouth
Swallows food rather than pushing it back out

key_points: Most babies are ready at around 6 months.
Look for all three signs together: sitting steadily, picking food up to their mouth, and swallowing it.
Born early? Ask your health visitor when to start.

title: Baby-led weaning, the safer way
summary: Finger foods from the start, following the BLISS trial's advice on iron, energy and choking.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: Baby-led weaning means offering finger foods and letting your baby feed themselves instead of spoon-feeding purées. Some families mix the two. The NHS says there's no right or wrong way, as long as your baby eats a wide variety of food.

sections.heading: The BLISS approach
paragraphs: BLISS is a version of baby-led weaning designed by researchers in New Zealand to address worries about iron, growth and choking. At each meal:
bullets: Offer food your baby can pick up and feed themselves.
Offer one high-iron food: red meat, beans, lentils or chickpeas, or iron-fortified cereal.
Offer one high-energy food, such as avocado, cheese, or nut butter on toast.
Make it soft enough to squash with the tongue against the roof of the mouth.
Avoid hard foods, small round foods, coin-shaped slices and foods that crumb in the mouth, such as rice crackers.

sections.heading: What the research found
paragraphs: In the BLISS trial of 206 babies, those weaned this way didn't choke more often than spoon-fed babies. About a third of babies in both groups choked at least once between 6 and 8 months, so how food is prepared matters whichever way you wean.

sections.heading: Every meal
bullets: Sit your baby upright and alert in a highchair, and always stay with them while they eat.
Let them decide how much to eat; never force them.
Breast milk or first infant formula stays the main drink until 12 months.
Offer sips of water from an open or free-flow cup with meals.
Babies under 12 months don't need snacks: offer milk if they seem hungry between meals.
Expect mess, and expect gagging: it's a normal reflex while learning (see Gagging or choking?).

sections.heading: Keep offering
paragraphs: It may take 10 tries or more for a baby to get used to a new food, flavour or texture. In one study, babies' intake of a vegetable they first disliked caught up with a liked one by about the 8th offering. The foods tracker counts tries for you.

checklist.text: A highchair where they sit upright
Everyone who feeds them knows the choking steps
An iron-rich food planned for each meal
An open or free-flow cup for water

key_points: Finger foods from the start, or mixed with spoon-feeding: both are fine.
At each meal: an iron-rich food, an energy-rich food, and nothing hard, round or crumbly.
Always sit them upright and stay with them while they eat.
Keep offering: it can take 10 tries or more.

title: Gagging or choking?
summary: How to tell them apart, and what to do if your child is choking.

sections.heading: Gagging is normal
paragraphs: Gagging is a normal reflex while babies learn to chew and swallow. It's noisy: watery eyes, the tongue pushed forward, retching or being sick, and sometimes a red face. Stay calm and let them work it out.

sections.heading: Choking is quiet
paragraphs: A choking child may be unable to cough, cry or breathe, and may start to look blue. On brown or black skin, look for blueness in the gums, inside the lips or in the fingernails.

sections.heading: Afterwards
paragraphs: Get medical help even if the object comes out: part of it may still be there, or they may have been hurt.

checklist.text: Read the choking steps with everyone who feeds them

card.title: If your child is choking
card.body: Shout for help and don't leave them. Under 1: lie them face down along your thigh, supporting the head, and give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades. If that doesn't work, lie them face up and give up to 5 chest thrusts with 2 fingers in the middle of the chest, just below the nipple line. Over 1: up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts. Call 999 if the blockage doesn't come out, and keep repeating until help arrives.
card.signpost: 999 if it doesn't clear · get checked even if it does

key_points: Gagging is noisy and normal while learning to eat.
Choking is quiet: they can't cough, cry or breathe.
Under 1: up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 chest thrusts; call 999 if it doesn't clear.
A short baby first aid course lets you practise.

links.title: First aid for a choking baby
First aid for a choking child

title: Foods to avoid, and how to cut risky ones
summary: What not to give yet, what to keep low, and how to prepare foods to lower the choking risk.

sections.heading: Not before 1 year
bullets: Honey.
Whole raisins or other whole dried fruit.
Cows' milk as the main drink (it's fine in cooking from 6 months).

sections.heading: Not before 5
bullets: Whole nuts and peanuts: crush or grind them instead.
Popcorn.
Rice drinks instead of breast milk, formula or cows' milk.

sections.heading: Not for babies and young children
bullets: Raw jelly cubes.
Raw or lightly cooked shellfish.
Shark, swordfish and marlin.
Mould-ripened soft cheeses such as brie, soft blue cheeses, ripened goats' cheese and unpasteurised cheese (unless cooked).
Raw or lightly cooked eggs without the British Lion stamp.
Slush ice drinks (age 7 and under).

sections.heading: Keep low
bullets: Salt: don't add it to food or cooking water, avoid stock cubes and gravy, and limit bacon, sausages, crisps, crackers and ready meals.
Added sugar and sweeteners, including honey, syrup, fruit juice and smoothies, for children 4 and under. Fruit is fine.

sections.heading: Cut to size
bullets: Small round fruits such as grapes, cherries, berries and cherry tomatoes: into quarters.
Melon and apple: slices, not small chunks.
Carrot, pepper, cucumber and celery: narrow batons.
Sausages: short strips. Meat: strips as thin as possible, with all bones removed. Fish: no bones.
Cheese: grated or in short, narrow strips. Bread: narrow strips.
Nuts and seeds: chopped, flaked or ground. Nut butter spread on food, never on its own.

key_points: No honey before 1, no whole nuts or popcorn before 5.
Quarter small round foods like grapes and cherry tomatoes.
No added salt or sugar.

title: Introducing allergens
summary: Which foods, when, how, and how to keep them going.

sections.heading: Which foods
paragraphs: The NHS lists foods that can trigger allergic reactions:
bullets: Cows' milk, eggs, and foods with gluten (wheat, barley, rye).
Nuts and peanuts (crushed, ground or as smooth nut butter), and seeds, especially sesame.
Soya, fish and shellfish.
Also beans, lentils and peas, celery, mustard, and sulphites in some dried fruit.

sections.heading: When
paragraphs: From around 6 months, alongside other foods. The NHS warns that delaying peanut and hen's egg beyond 6 to 12 months may increase the risk of allergy to them; trials such as LEAP and EAT suggest that eating peanut and egg early and regularly lowers the chance of allergy to them.

sections.heading: How
bullets: One new allergen at a time, in a very small amount, so you can spot any reaction.
Reactions usually start within minutes but can take up to 2 hours, or up to 3 days for cows' milk.
Once a food is tolerated, keep it in the usual diet. The foods tracker reminds you if one hasn't been offered for a week.
Don't cut out major foods such as milk without advice.

sections.heading: Talk to your GP or health visitor first if
bullets: Your baby already has a diagnosed food allergy or eczema.
There's a family history of food allergies, eczema, asthma or hay fever.

card.title: Signs of a serious reaction
card.body: Call 999 straight away if your child has breathing problems, a swollen throat or tongue, or suddenly becomes very unwell after eating. For milder signs, such as an itchy rash, swollen lips, watery eyes or being sick, talk to your GP or health visitor before offering that food again.
card.signpost: 999 in an emergency · GP or health visitor

key_points: Introduce egg, peanut and the other allergens from around 6 months.
One new allergen at a time, on a day without other allergens, in a small amount.
Once it's tolerated, keep it in their usual diet.
Swollen throat or tongue, or breathing problems: call 999.

title: Drinks and cups
summary: Water, cups, and moving to cows' milk at 1.

sections.heading: From around 6 months
bullets: Offer sips of water from a cup or beaker with meals. Tap water doesn't need boiling from 6 months.
An open or free-flow cup without a valve helps babies learn to sip and is better for their teeth.
Breast milk or first infant formula stays the main drink.
Babies don't need fruit juice or smoothies. Squash and fizzy drinks aren't suitable.

sections.heading: From 1 year
bullets: Whole or semi-skimmed pasteurised cows' milk can be the main drink. Skimmed and 1% milk aren't suitable as the main drink before 5.
Unsweetened, calcium-fortified soya, oat or almond drinks can be part of a balanced diet. No rice drinks before 5.
Formula milks aren't needed, and feeding from a bottle should be discouraged.
Move from a lidded beaker to an open cup as soon as they're ready.

checklist.text: Water in an open or free-flow cup with meals
Cows' milk as the main drink (from 1 year)
Moved from bottles to cups (from 1 year)

key_points: Water in an open or free-flow cup with meals from around 6 months.
Breast milk or formula is the main drink until 1; then whole cows' milk.
No juice, squash or rice drinks.

title: Vitamins
summary: Which vitamins the NHS recommends, from birth to 5.

bullets: Breastfed babies: a daily vitamin D supplement from birth, even if the mother takes vitamin D herself.
From 6 months to 5 years: a daily supplement with vitamins A, C and D.
Babies having more than 500ml of infant formula a day don't need supplements: formula is already fortified.
If your family qualifies for Healthy Start, the vitamin drops are free.

paragraphs: A pharmacist or your health visitor can tell you which product to buy.

checklist.text: Daily vitamins sorted, if they need them

key_points: Breastfed babies: vitamin D every day from birth.
From 6 months to 5 years: vitamins A, C and D daily, unless they have more than 500ml of formula a day.

links.title: Healthy Start
links.note: Free vitamins and help buying food, if you qualify

title: Teeth and brushing
summary: Brushing from the first tooth, toothpaste by age, and the first dentist visit.

bullets: Start brushing as soon as the first milk tooth comes through, usually at around 6 months.
Brush twice a day for about 2 minutes, including last thing at night.
Under 3: a smear of children's fluoride toothpaste with at least 1,000ppm fluoride.
3 to 6: a pea-sized amount of toothpaste with 1,000 to 1,500ppm fluoride.
Spit out the toothpaste afterwards, but don't rinse: rinsing washes the fluoride away.
Take them to the dentist when their first teeth come through, or before they turn 1. NHS dental care is free for children.

checklist.text: Brushing twice a day
First dentist visit

key_points: Brush twice a day from the first tooth.
A smear of fluoride toothpaste under 3, pea-sized from 3; spit, don't rinse.
First dentist visit when teeth come through, or before 1. It's free on the NHS.

links.title: Caring for your baby or toddler's teeth

title: Sun safety
summary: Shade, hats and sunscreen for babies and young children.

bullets: Keep babies under 6 months out of direct strong sunlight.
Spend time in the shade, especially from 11am to 3pm.
Cover up with clothes and a wide-brimmed hat that shades the face, neck and ears, from March to October.
Use sunscreen of at least SPF 30 with at least 4-star UVA protection, and reapply often, especially after swimming or towel drying.

checklist.text: A wide-brimmed sun hat
SPF 30+ sunscreen with 4-star UVA

key_points: Keep babies under 6 months out of strong direct sun.
Shade, a wide-brimmed hat, and SPF 30+ with 4-star UVA.

title: Potty training
summary: When to start, what you need, and what to expect.

sections.heading: When
paragraphs: Almost all children can be potty trained between 18 months and 2 and a half. Signs they're getting aware:
bullets: They tell you they need a wee or poo.
They tell you when they're wet or dirty.
They fidget, go quiet or make faces.

paragraphs: Some children don't show these signs, and that's okay too: you can still start.

sections.heading: Getting started
bullets: Pick a calm time and tell them what's changing.
Switch to pants in the day, and keep nappies for naps and night.
Offer the potty at regular times: after waking, after meals and before bed.
Praise the effort, and let them practise flushing and washing hands.
Accidents are a normal part of learning: stay calm, clean up together and move on.
Dry nights usually follow dry days in time, so they don't need teaching.

checklist.text: A potty, or a toilet seat with a step
Pants and clothes that are easy to pull down
Spare clothes in the changing bag
Regular potty times

key_points: Most children are ready between 18 months and 2 and a half.
Pants in the day, nappies for naps and nights at first.
Accidents are normal: stay calm.

title: Childcare and funded hours
summary: Help with childcare costs in England, and getting ready for nursery.

paragraphs: In England, working families and others can get help with childcare costs:
bullets: 15 and 30 hours support for children aged 9 months to 4 years.
Tax-Free Childcare: the government adds £2 for every £8 you pay in.
Universal Credit childcare: working families can claim back up to 85% of eligible costs.

paragraphs: Who qualifies and when to apply depend on your circumstances, so use the Childcare Checker well before you need a place.

checklist.text: Checked what support you can get
Visited nurseries or childminders
Planned settling-in sessions

key_points: Funded hours can start from 9 months in England.
Check what you can get well before you need a place.

title: Starting school
summary: When they can start reception in England, and the dates to apply by.

paragraphs: In England, children can start reception in the September after their 4th birthday. You apply through your local council, even for schools in another council area.
bullets: Applications open in the autumn before; check your council's dates.
The national closing date is 15 January.
Primary offers are made on 16 April, or the next working day.

checklist.text: Visited schools or open days
Applied by 15 January
Accepted a place

key_points: Reception starts the September after their 4th birthday.
Apply to your council by 15 January.
Offers come on 16 April (or the next working day).

title: Childproofing the home
summary: What to do as your baby starts to roll, crawl, climb and explore.

sections.heading: Falls
bullets: Change nappies on a mat on the floor, and never leave a baby alone on a raised surface.
Keep bouncers and car seats on the floor, not on tables or worktops.
Fit stair gates at the top and bottom of the stairs until your child is at least 2.
Use a 5-point harness in the highchair and pram every time.
Keep low furniture away from windows, and fit window locks or catches.

sections.heading: Burns and scalds
bullets: Run cold water into the bath before hot, and test it with your elbow.
Keep hot drinks out of reach: they can still scald 15 minutes after they're made.
Use a cordless kettle or one with a short flex, and turn pan handles inwards.

sections.heading: Swallowing and poisoning
bullets: Keep button batteries and magnets well away: swallowed, they can cause serious internal injuries.
Lock medicines away or keep them high up, out of reach and sight.
Store laundry capsules, dishwasher tablets, cleaning products and e-cigarette refills out of reach.

sections.heading: Water and cords
bullets: Babies can drown in 5cm of water: stay within reach at bath time and empty the bath straight after.
Empty paddling pools after use, and fence off or cover ponds.
Tie up curtain and blind cords on a cleat hook, and don't leave cords or drawstring bags lying around.

checklist.text: Stair gates at the top and bottom of the stairs
Window locks or catches fitted
Blind and curtain cords tied up out of reach
Medicines and cleaning products locked away or up high
Button batteries and magnets out of reach
Low furniture moved away from windows

key_points: Stair gates top and bottom, window locks, cords tied up.
Button batteries, magnets, medicines and cleaning products out of reach.
Babies can drown in 5cm of water: stay within reach at bath time.

title: Car seats
summary: The UK rules for child car seats, and keeping babies rear-facing.

paragraphs: Children must use a child car seat until they're 12 years old or 135cm tall, whichever comes first.

sections.heading: Height-based (i-Size) seats
bullets: Rear-facing until your child is over 15 months old.
Look for the approval label R129 with a capital E in a circle.

sections.heading: Weight-based seats
bullets: Group 0+ (up to 13kg): rear-facing baby carrier or seat with a harness.
Group 1 (about 9 to 18kg): rear- or forward-facing seat with a harness or safety shield.
Look for the approval label ECE R44 with a capital E in a circle.

sections.heading: Fitting
bullets: Turn off the front airbag before fitting a rear-facing seat in a front seat.
Never fit a child seat in a side-facing seat.
Use the seat belt or ISOFIX fittings the seat was designed for.

checklist.text: Seat has an R129 or ECE R44 label
Rear-facing (i-Size: until over 15 months)
Front airbag off if the seat is in the front

key_points: A child car seat until 12 years or 135cm.
i-Size seats: rear-facing until over 15 months.
Front airbag off if a rear-facing seat is in the front.

title: Toddler meals
summary: What a balanced day looks like from 1 to 5.

sections.heading: Each day
bullets: Fruit and vegetables at every meal, in a variety of colours.
Starchy foods such as bread, rice, pasta and potatoes. Under 2s shouldn't have only wholegrain.
At least 350ml of milk, or two servings of milk-based foods like cheese or yoghurt. Full-fat until 2.
Protein: at least 2 portions from beans, lentils or tofu, or 1 from meat, fish or eggs.
At least 1 portion of oily fish a week.

sections.heading: Keep low
bullets: No need to add salt: most foods already contain enough.
Sugary foods and drinks only with meals, not as snacks or before bed. No fizzy drinks.
Water and milk as the main drinks.

sections.heading: Fussy eating
paragraphs: It's common for toddlers to eat only one or two fruits or vegetables at first. Keep offering small amounts of others so they can learn to like new tastes and textures.

key_points: Fruit and vegetables at every meal.
About 350ml of milk a day, full-fat until 2.
Sugary foods only with meals; no added salt.

title: Talking and sharing books
summary: Everyday ways to build language, from chatting at nappy changes to stories.

bullets: From birth: chat about what you're doing as you feed, change and bathe your baby.
From 6 months: look at books together. You don't have to read the words; talk about what you can see.
From 12 months: books and toys that make a noise help listening.
From 18 months: repetition helps children remember words, so reading favourites again and again is good.
From 2: switch off the TV and radio when you're talking together: background noise makes listening harder.
Talk in whichever language feels comfortable to you: knowing another language helps English too.

sections.heading: Dummies
paragraphs: It's hard to learn to talk with a dummy in, so offer it only for sleep from 6 months and aim to stop by 12 months.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends reading aloud with children from infancy: shared reading builds language and early literacy, and back-and-forth conversation matters as much as the words.

checklist.text: A book together most days
Joined the local library

key_points: Chat through everyday routines from birth.
Look at books together from 6 months: talk about the pictures.
Switch off background TV and radio when you're talking.

title: Safer sleep
summary: How to lower the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) at every sleep.

sections.heading: Every sleep
bullets: Lie your baby on their back to sleep, in the feet-to-foot position (feet touching the end of the cot).
Use their own clear, flat, firm sleep space, such as a cot or Moses basket, with a firm, flat mattress.
Keep them in the same room as you for every sleep for at least the first 6 months.
Keep the room between 16 and 20°C: babies are at higher risk if they get too hot.
Keep your baby smoke-free, in pregnancy and after birth.
Any amount of breastfeeding lowers the risk.

sections.heading: Avoid
bullets: Sleeping on a sofa or in an armchair with your baby.
Pillows, duvets, cot bumpers, loose blankets or soft toys in the cot.
Products that keep a baby in one position, such as wedges, straps, pods or nests.
Sharing a bed if your baby was born before 37 weeks, or if you or your partner smoke, have drunk alcohol or taken drugs.
Letting your baby sleep in a car seat for long.

checklist.text: A clear, flat, firm cot or Moses basket
Sleeping in the same room as you
Room thermometer (16 to 20°C)

key_points: On their back, feet to foot, in a clear cot.
Same room as you for at least 6 months.
Never sleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair.

title: When to get urgent help
summary: The signs that mean 999 or A&E, and when to call NHS 111.

sections.heading: Call 999 or go to A&E if your child
bullets: Has swollen lips, tongue or throat with difficulty swallowing or talking.
Is breathing very fast or finding it hard to breathe: they may grunt or suck their tummy in as they breathe.
Has blue, grey, pale or blotchy (mottled) skin, lips or tongue. On black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands or soles of the feet.
Has skin that feels cold or damp (clammy) to touch.
Has a rash that does not fade when you press it.
Has a very high temperature: 38°C or higher under 3 months, or 39°C or higher at 3 to 6 months.
Has a very low temperature (below 36°C), or feels cold to touch or is shivery.
Has a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry.
Has fainted, is difficult to wake or can't be woken.
Has not had a pee in the past 12 hours, or is having a seizure (fit).

sections.heading: Call NHS 111 if
bullets: You're worried about any of their symptoms or don't know what to do.
They're 3 months to 5 years old and a temperature of 38°C or higher has lasted more than 5 days.

paragraphs: Trust your instincts: if you think something is seriously wrong, get medical help straight away.

card.title: In an emergency
card.body: Call 999 if your child has stopped breathing, is struggling to breathe, can't be woken, has a fit, has a rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass on it, or is under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher.
card.signpost: 999 in an emergency · NHS 111 for urgent advice

key_points: 999 or A&E for breathing difficulty, blue or grey skin, a fit, can't be woken, a rash that doesn't fade, or 38°C or higher under 3 months (39°C at 3 to 6 months).
NHS 111 whenever you're worried or don't know what to do.
Trust your instincts.
